name: Aye-aye
facts: It taps on tree bark with an extra-long, skinny middle finger and listens for hollow tunnels made by grubs.
Once it finds a grub, it gnaws a hole with its ever-growing rodent-like incisors and hooks the larva out with that same finger.
It is the world's largest nocturnal primate.
In some Malagasy folklore it is considered an omen of bad luck, which has led to it being killed on sight in places.

name: Saiga antelope
habitat: Steppes of Kazakhstan, Russia, Mongolia and Uzbekistan
facts: Its huge, floppy, trunk-like nose helps filter dust in summer and warm frigid air in winter.
In 2015 more than 200,000 saigas died within weeks from a bacterial infection linked to unusually warm, humid weather.
Thanks to conservation efforts, numbers in Kazakhstan rebounded dramatically and the species was downlisted from Critically Endangered in 2023.
Males' translucent, amber-coloured horns have made them a target for poaching for traditional medicine.

name: Okapi
habitat: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
facts: Despite its zebra-striped legs, its closest living relative is the giraffe.
Its tongue is long enough to clean its own eyelids and ears.
It was unknown to Western science until the early 1900s, earning it the nickname 'African unicorn'.
Okapis communicate partly with infrasonic calls below the range of human hearing.

name: Blobfish
habitat: Deep waters off southeastern Australia and New Zealand
facts: In its deep-sea home it looks like a fairly normal fish; the famous 'blob' look comes from decompression when it is hauled to the surface.
Its body is mostly gelatinous flesh slightly less dense than water, letting it hover just above the sea floor without spending energy swimming.
It lives at depths of roughly 600 to 1,200 metres.
It was voted the world's ugliest animal in a 2013 online poll by the Ugly Animal Preservation Society.

name: Pink fairy armadillo
habitat: Sandy plains and grasslands of central Argentina
facts: At around 10 cm long, it is the smallest armadillo in the world.
Its pinkish shell is only attached to its body along a thin strip down the back.
It spends nearly its entire life underground, 'swimming' through sand with large front claws.
The flat, vertical plate at its rear may be used to pack down soil behind it as it digs.

name: Blue dragon sea slug
habitat: Floating on the surface of temperate and tropical oceans worldwide
facts: It floats upside down on the ocean surface, held up by a swallowed air bubble in its stomach.
It eats venomous Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells in its own fingerlike appendages for defense.
Because it concentrates the stingers, its sting can be more painful than the man o' war's.
Its blue-and-silver countershading camouflages it from predators both above and below.

name: Shoebill
facts: Its enormous shoe-shaped bill can be over 20 cm long and ends in a sharp hook.
It is famous for standing motionless for long periods before lunging at prey such as lungfish.
It cools its eggs in hot weather by scooping up water in its bill and pouring it over the nest.
Shoebills often clatter their bills together loudly as a form of communication.

name: Axolotl
facts: It stays in its aquatic larval form its whole life, a trait called neoteny.
It can regrow entire limbs, parts of its spinal cord, heart and even parts of its brain.
In the wild it is critically endangered and survives almost only in the canals of Xochimilco.
Its feathery external gills give it a permanent 'smiling with a crown' look.

name: Star-nosed mole
habitat: Wetlands of eastern Canada and the northeastern United States
facts: Its nose is ringed by 22 fleshy tentacles packed with over 25,000 touch receptors called Eimer's organs.
It can identify and eat a food item in as little as about a quarter of a second, among the fastest foragers known.
It can smell underwater by blowing out air bubbles and re-inhaling them.
It is a strong swimmer and often forages in streams and ponds.

name: Fossa
facts: It looks like a small cougar but is actually most closely related to mongooses.
It is the largest native carnivore on Madagascar.
Lemurs make up a large part of its diet, and it is an agile climber that can descend trees headfirst.
Its flexible ankles let it move through trees almost like a squirrel.

name: Gerenuk
habitat: Dry scrublands of the Horn of Africa and East Africa
facts: It stands upright on its hind legs to browse leaves that other antelopes can't reach.
Its name comes from a Somali word meaning 'giraffe-necked'.
It can survive without drinking water, getting moisture from the plants it eats.
Only the males have horns.

name: Markhor
habitat: Mountains of Pakistan, Afghanistan and Central Asia
facts: Males grow dramatic corkscrew-shaped horns that can reach over 1.5 metres long.
It is the national animal of Pakistan.
Its name is often translated from Persian as 'snake-eater', though it is a plant-eating goat.
It climbs steep cliffs and even trees to reach food.

name: Dumbo octopus
facts: It is named for its ear-like fins, which it flaps to 'fly' through the water.
Members of this group live deeper than almost any other octopus, recorded at around 7,000 metres.
Unlike most octopuses, it has no ink sac, since there is little need for ink in the dark deep sea.
It swallows its prey whole rather than tearing it apart.

name: Yeti crab
habitat: Hydrothermal vents in the South Pacific
facts: It was discovered only in 2005 near Easter Island.
Its arms are covered in hair-like setae that host colonies of bacteria.
Scientists think it may 'farm' these bacteria and eat them.
It is essentially blind, with only vestigial eyes.

name: Thorny devil
habitat: Deserts of central and western Australia
facts: Grooves between its spines draw water toward its mouth by capillary action, letting it 'drink' with its skin from damp sand.
It eats almost nothing but ants, sometimes thousands in one meal.
A spiny 'false head' on the back of its neck may fool predators when it tucks its real head down.
It can change colour from pale yellows to dark browns depending on temperature.

name: Tardigrade
habitat: Almost everywhere: moss, soil, oceans and mountains worldwide
facts: These microscopic animals, often called water bears, are usually under 1 mm long.
In a dried-out 'tun' state they can survive extreme cold, radiation and even the vacuum of space.
In 2007 tardigrades survived exposure to open space on the FOTON-M3 mission.
They have eight stubby legs, each tipped with claws.

name: Narwhal
habitat: Arctic waters around Greenland, Canada and Russia
facts: Its 'tusk' is actually a tooth that grows through its upper lip, sometimes reaching 3 metres.
The tusk contains millions of nerve endings and may sense changes in water.
Narwhals can dive more than 1,500 metres deep.
Medieval traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns.

name: Proboscis monkey
habitat: Mangrove and riverine forests of Borneo
facts: Males have huge, pendulous noses that may amplify their calls and attract females.
It is an excellent swimmer, with partially webbed feet.
It has a complex, multi-chambered stomach to digest leaves, giving it a pot-bellied look.
It is found only on the island of Borneo.

name: Babirusa
habitat: Rainforests of Sulawesi and nearby Indonesian islands
facts: Males' upper tusks grow up through the top of the snout and curve back toward the forehead.
Its name means 'pig-deer' in Malay.
If the tusks aren't worn down, they can keep curving and in rare cases may even pierce the skull.
It is often seen wallowing in mud, but unlike many pigs it rarely roots in the ground with its snout.

name: Sunda colugo
facts: Despite the name 'flying lemur', it is neither a lemur nor can it truly fly; it glides.
A membrane stretches from its neck to the tips of its fingers, toes and tail.
It can glide over 100 metres between trees.
Colugos are among the closest living relatives of primates.

name: Matamata
habitat: Slow-moving waters of the Amazon and Orinoco basins
facts: Its flattened, leaf-like head and rough shell camouflage it as a pile of debris.
It feeds by suddenly opening its huge mouth to create a vacuum that sucks in fish.
It breathes through a long, snorkel-like snout while staying hidden underwater.
It has very poor eyesight and senses prey with sensitive skin flaps on its neck.

name: Gharial
habitat: Rivers of northern India and Nepal
facts: Its extremely long, thin snout is lined with over 100 sharp interlocking teeth, ideal for catching fish.
Adult males grow a bulbous knob on the snout tip called a 'ghara', after an Indian pot.
The ghara lets males make a buzzing sound and blow bubbles to attract females.
It is critically endangered, with only a few hundred breeding adults left in the wild.

name: Kakapo
facts: It is the world's only flightless parrot and the heaviest parrot.
It is nocturnal and has a strong musty, sweet smell.
Males attract mates with deep 'booming' calls that can travel several kilometres.
Every surviving kakapo is individually named and tracked; the population is only around 250 birds.

name: Mantis shrimp
facts: Its club-like claws strike so fast that they create collapsing cavitation bubbles, hitting prey with a second shockwave.
A single punch can crack crab shells and even aquarium glass.
Its eyes have up to 16 types of photoreceptors and can see polarized light.
Its club is made of a layered material so tough it has inspired new body armor designs.

name: Leafy seadragon
habitat: Coastal waters of southern and western Australia
facts: Its body is covered in leaf-shaped appendages that make it look like drifting seaweed.
Like seahorses, the male carries the eggs, attached to the underside of his tail.
It moves using tiny, almost transparent fins on its neck and back.
It is the marine emblem of the state of South Australia.

name: Hoatzin
habitat: Swamps and riverbanks of the Amazon and Orinoco basins
facts: Chicks are born with two claws on each wing, which they use to climb branches.
It digests leaves by fermentation in a large crop, giving it a manure-like smell and the nickname 'stinkbird'.
Chicks escape predators by dropping into the water and swimming, then climbing back up.
It is the national bird of Guyana.

name: Tufted deer
habitat: Mountain forests of China and Myanmar
facts: Males have tiny horns that are often hidden by a tuft of hair on the forehead.
Males also have long, fang-like upper canine teeth.
It barks when alarmed.
It is mostly active at dawn and dusk.

name: Pangolin
facts: It is the only mammal covered in large, overlapping keratin scales.
When threatened, it rolls into a tight armored ball.
Its sticky tongue can be longer than its body and is anchored near its pelvis.
Pangolins are thought to be among the most trafficked mammals in the world.

name: Sea pig
facts: It is actually a type of sea cucumber, not a pig.
It walks across the seabed on tube feet that are inflated with water.
It feeds by sifting nutrients from mud on the ocean floor.
Sea pigs can gather in huge herds of hundreds of individuals.

name: Irrawaddy dolphin
habitat: Coasts and rivers of South and Southeast Asia
facts: It has a rounded, blunt head with no beak, giving it a smiling look.
It sometimes spits jets of water from its mouth, possibly to herd fish.
In Myanmar, some groups traditionally cooperated with fishermen to drive fish into nets.
Several freshwater populations are critically endangered.

name: Maned wolf
facts: Despite its name and look, it is not a true wolf; it is in its own genus.
Its very long legs help it see over tall grass.
Nearly half of its diet is fruit, especially the 'wolf apple' (lobeira).
Its urine has a strong smell often compared to cannabis.

name: Raccoon dog
facts: It looks like a raccoon but is a member of the dog family.
It is the only member of the dog family known to go into a hibernation-like winter sleep.
In Japan it is known as the tanuki, a famous shapeshifting trickster in folklore.
Unlike most dogs, it rarely barks.

name: Dhole
habitat: Forests of South and Southeast Asia
facts: Packs communicate using distinctive whistles, earning it the name 'whistling dog'.
Packs can take down prey as large as sambar deer and even fend off tigers.
Unlike most pack animals, dholes let pups eat first at a kill.
It is endangered, with an estimated few thousand adults left in the wild.

name: Solenodon
habitat: Forests of Hispaniola (Haiti and Dominican Republic)
facts: It is one of very few venomous mammals, delivering venom through grooved teeth.
Its lineage split from other mammals roughly 70 million years ago, around the time of the dinosaurs.
It survived the asteroid impact era, but now struggles against introduced dogs and cats.
Its long, flexible snout is attached to the skull by a ball-and-socket joint.

name: Bush dog
habitat: Forests and wetlands of Central and South America
facts: It has short legs and a stocky body and looks a bit like a cross between a dog and an otter.
It is an excellent swimmer and has partially webbed feet.
Packs hunt prey much larger than themselves, such as pacas and capybaras.
It is rarely seen in the wild and was first described from fossils before living animals were known to science.

name: Quokka
facts: Its upturned mouth makes it look like it is smiling, earning it the title 'world's happiest animal'.
Rottnest Island was named 'rat nest island' by a Dutch explorer who mistook quokkas for giant rats.
It is a small marsupial, about the size of a house cat.
It can survive for long periods without water by eating succulent plants.

name: Numbat
facts: It eats almost exclusively termites, up to about 20,000 a day.
Unlike most marsupials, females have no pouch; the young cling to their mother's belly.
It is one of the few marsupials that is active during the day, matching termite activity.
It is the official animal emblem of Western Australia.

name: Echidna
facts: It is one of only a few mammals that lay eggs.
The female lays a single leathery egg directly into a temporary pouch.
Babies, called puggles, hatch without spines.
It has electroreceptors in its snout that may help it detect prey.

name: Southern cassowary
habitat: Rainforests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia
facts: Each foot has a dagger-like inner claw up to about 12 cm long.
The tall, helmet-like casque on its head may help it push through vegetation or amplify sounds.
Males incubate the eggs and raise the chicks alone.
It plays a key role in spreading the seeds of rainforest fruit trees.

name: Takahe
facts: It was believed extinct until it was rediscovered in 1948 in the Murchison Mountains.
It is a large, flightless bird in the rail family.
It feeds by holding grass stalks with one foot and nibbling the soft base.
Its population is slowly growing thanks to intensive conservation.

name: Kea
facts: It is the world's only alpine parrot.
It is famous for its curiosity and tool-solving intelligence.
Kea are notorious for pulling apart car wiper blades and rubber seals.
Its plain olive-green feathers hide bright orange-red underwings.

name: Tuatara
facts: Although it looks like a lizard, it is the only surviving member of an ancient reptile order, Rhynchocephalia.
It has a 'third eye' (parietal eye) on top of its head, visible in hatchlings.
It can live over 100 years.
It is active at lower temperatures than most reptiles.

name: Long-eared jerboa
habitat: Deserts of Mongolia and northwestern China
facts: Its ears are about one third larger than its head, proportionally among the largest of any rodent.
It is nocturnal and was first filmed in the wild in 2007.
It catches flying insects at night.
It is in its own genus, with no close living relatives.

name: Sand cat
habitat: Deserts of North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia
facts: It is the only cat species that lives mainly in true deserts.
Thick fur on its paw pads protects it from hot sand and leaves faint tracks.
It can survive without drinking, getting water from prey.
It digs burrows to escape the heat.

name: Pallas's cat
habitat: Grasslands and steppes of Central Asia
facts: It has the densest fur of any cat.
Its round pupils are unlike the slit pupils of most small cats.
Its short legs and flat face give it a famously grumpy expression.
It lives at elevations up to around 5,000 metres.

name: Fishing cat
habitat: Wetlands of South and Southeast Asia
facts: It is a strong swimmer and dives for fish.
Its front paws are partly webbed.
It sometimes taps the water surface with its paw to lure fish.
It is the state animal of West Bengal, India.

name: Clouded leopard
habitat: Forests from the Himalayas to Southeast Asia
facts: It has the longest canine teeth relative to skull size of any living cat.
It can climb down trees headfirst and hang upside down from branches.
Its large, cloud-shaped markings give it its name.
Its legs are short and its tail is very long, helping it balance in trees.

name: Serval
facts: It has the longest legs relative to body size of any cat.
Its large ears can hear rodents moving underground.
It can leap more than 3 metres into the air to catch birds.
It has a high hunting success rate, around 50%.

name: Caracal
habitat: Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia
facts: It is famous for long black ear tufts.
It can leap up to 3 metres to swat birds out of the air.
Historically it was trained in India and Persia to hunt birds.
Its name comes from a Turkish word meaning 'black ear'.

name: Margay
habitat: Forests of Central and South America
facts: It can rotate its ankles 180 degrees, allowing it to climb down trees headfirst.
It can hang from branches by just one hind foot.
It is one of the most tree-dwelling cats in the Americas.
It has very large eyes for its size, helping it hunt at night.

name: Kinkajou
habitat: Rainforests of Central and South America
facts: It is a relative of the raccoon, not a primate.
It has a prehensile tail it uses to grip branches.
Its long tongue helps it eat nectar and honey, earning it the name 'honey bear'.
It is an important pollinator for some plants.

name: Binturong
habitat: Forests of South and Southeast Asia
facts: It is also called a bearcat but is neither a bear nor a cat.
It smells like buttered popcorn due to a compound in its urine.
It has a prehensile tail, unusual among carnivores of the Old World.
It helps spread seeds of strangler figs.

name: White-nosed coati
habitat: Forests of the southwestern US, Mexico and Central America
facts: It has a long, flexible nose for rooting in leaf litter.
Females and young live in groups called bands.
It holds its long, striped tail upright while walking.
It is related to raccoons.

name: Southern tamandua
facts: This tree-climbing anteater uses a prehensile tail.
It can eat thousands of ants and termites a day.
It is nicknamed the 'stinker of the forest' for its strong odour.
When threatened, it rears up on its hind legs and slashes with long claws.

name: Aardvark
facts: Its name means 'earth pig' in Afrikaans.
It can dig burrows incredibly fast with its powerful claws.
It has teeth with no enamel that keep growing.
Its abandoned burrows provide shelter for many other animals.

name: Aardwolf
facts: It is a hyena relative that eats mainly termites.
It can eat over 200,000 termites in a single night.
Its teeth are small and weak, suited for termites rather than meat.
Its name means 'earth wolf' in Afrikaans.

name: Bat-eared fox
habitat: Savannas of eastern and southern Africa
facts: Its huge ears help it hear insects underground.
It eats mostly termites and other insects.
It has more teeth than most mammals, up to 50.
Males help care for the young.

name: Rock hyrax
habitat: Rocky areas of Africa and the Middle East
facts: Despite its rodent-like look, it is related to elephants and manatees.
It has sweaty foot pads that help it grip rocks.
It basks in the sun because it has poor control of its body temperature.
Its fossilized urine, called hyraceum, has been used in perfumes.

name: Springhare
facts: It hops like a small kangaroo.
It digs complex burrows and blocks entrances with soil.
Its eyes reflect light brightly at night.
It can leap up to about 2 metres in one jump.

name: Giant pangolin
habitat: Forests and savannas of central Africa
facts: It is the largest pangolin species.
It has a tongue that can reach over 40 cm.
It can break open termite mounds with its strong claws.
It is endangered due to poaching.

name: Elephant shrew
facts: Despite its name it is more closely related to elephants than to shrews.
It has a long, flexible nose.
It can run up to about 28 km/h.
It clears trails through leaf litter to escape predators.

name: Golden-rumped elephant shrew
facts: It has a striking golden patch on its rump.
It builds nests of leaves on the forest floor.
It feeds on insects and other invertebrates.
It is endangered due to habitat loss.

name: Hamerkop
habitat: Wetlands of sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar
facts: It builds enormous domed nests up to about 1.5 metres across, made of thousands of sticks.
Its name means 'hammerhead' in Afrikaans, after the shape of its head and crest.
Other animals, such as owls, snakes and genets, often move into its huge nests.
Groups sometimes perform 'false mounting' displays that are not actually mating.

name: Common potoo
habitat: Forests of Central and South America
facts: By day it perches motionless on a branch stub, looking exactly like part of the tree.
It can watch for threats with its eyes closed, peering through small notches in its eyelids.
Its haunting, descending call has inspired many folk legends.
It catches flying insects at night with a huge gaping mouth.

name: Tawny frogmouth
facts: It is often mistaken for an owl but is more closely related to nightjars.
When threatened, it freezes with its beak pointed up, mimicking a broken branch.
It catches insects with its wide, frog-like mouth.
Pairs often stay together for life.

name: Kagu
facts: It is nearly flightless and in its own family.
It has unique 'nasal corns', flaps that cover its nostrils, found in no other bird.
Its call sounds like a barking dog.
It is the national bird of New Caledonia.

name: Secretary bird
facts: It hunts on foot, stamping prey like snakes with powerful kicks.
Its kick can strike with a force about five times its own body weight.
The crest of long feathers on its head may have reminded people of quill pens behind a clerk's ear.
It appears on the coat of arms of South Africa.

name: New Zealand rock wren
habitat: Alpine zones of New Zealand's South Island
facts: It is one of only two surviving species of New Zealand wren.
It is considered New Zealand's only true alpine bird, living above the treeline year-round.
It bobs its body up and down constantly.
It can survive harsh alpine winters, possibly by sheltering under snow.

name: Wrybill
facts: It is the only bird in the world with a beak that bends sideways.
Its beak always curves to the right.
It uses the bent beak to reach insect larvae under river stones.
It breeds only on braided riverbeds of the South Island.

name: Southern ground hornbill
habitat: Savannas of southern and eastern Africa
facts: It spends most of its time walking on the ground.
Its booming call can be heard up to 3 km away.
It can live for decades, possibly more than 50 years in captivity.
It hunts snakes, tortoises and even hares.

name: Hyacinth macaw
facts: It is the largest flying parrot species by length.
Its powerful beak can crack coconuts and hard palm nuts.
It often eats palm nuts that have passed through cattle, making them easier to crack.
Its bright yellow eye rings and jaw patches contrast with its cobalt blue feathers.

name: Bearded vulture
habitat: Mountains of Europe, Africa and Asia
facts: Its diet is about 70-90% bone.
It drops bones from height onto rocks to break them into swallowable pieces.
It stains its feathers orange-red by bathing in iron-rich mud.
Its stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve bone.

name: Sunbittern
habitat: Tropical forests of Central and South America
facts: When threatened, it spreads its wings to reveal large eyespots.
It is in its own family, most closely related to the kagu.
It hunts fish and insects along forest streams.

name: Oilbird
habitat: Caves of northern South America and Trinidad
facts: It is the world's only nocturnal flying fruit-eating bird.
It uses echolocation clicks to navigate in pitch-dark caves.
Chicks become very fat, once harvested for oil, giving the bird its name.
It is thought to locate fruit at night partly by smell.

name: Helmeted hornbill
facts: Its casque is solid, unlike the hollow casques of most hornbills.
Males use their casques in mid-air head-butting contests.
Its casque has been carved like ivory, driving heavy poaching.
Its call is a series of hoots ending in maniacal laughter-like cackles.

name: Marabou stork
facts: It has one of the largest wingspans of any land bird, up to about 3 metres.
It has a bare head and a pink inflatable throat sac.
It often scavenges alongside vultures.
It sometimes excretes on its legs to cool down.

name: Bearded reedling
facts: Males have black 'moustaches', not beards.
It changes its digestive system between seasons, switching from insects to seeds.
It swallows tiny stones to help grind seeds in winter.
It is in a family of its own.

name: Superb lyrebird
facts: It can mimic almost any sound, including other birds, camera shutters and chainsaws.
Males display with a spectacular lyre-shaped tail.
It appears on the Australian 10-cent coin.
Males build display mounds in the forest.

name: Jabiru
habitat: Wetlands of Central and South America
facts: It is one of the tallest flying birds in South America.
Its name comes from a Tupi-Guarani word meaning 'swollen neck'.
It builds huge nests high in trees.
It wades shallow waters to catch fish and frogs.

name: Horned screamer
facts: It has a long, spine-like horn growing from its forehead.
It has two sharp spurs on each wing.
Its loud calls can be heard from far away.
It is related to ducks and geese.

name: Great potoo
habitat: Rainforests of Central and South America
facts: It has a huge mouth relative to its head.
It perches upright and still, blending into tree branches.
Its growling call is loud and eerie.
It hunts large insects at night.

name: Guianan cock-of-the-rock
habitat: Rocky forests of northern South America
facts: Males are bright orange with a half-moon crest that covers their bill.
Males gather in leks to display for females.
Females build nests of mud on rock faces.
It feeds mainly on fruit.

name: Satin bowerbird
facts: Males build stick bowers decorated with blue objects to attract females.
Males collect blue items like flowers, feathers and bottle caps.
Males take several years to reach their adult glossy blue-black plumage.
Some males paint bowers with chewed plant material.

name: Barreleye fish
habitat: Deep waters of the North Pacific
facts: It has a transparent, fluid-filled dome over its head.
Its tubular green eyes sit inside the dome and can rotate to look upward or forward.
What look like eyes on its face are actually its nostrils.
Scientists think it may steal food caught in the stinging tentacles of siphonophores.

name: Frilled shark
habitat: Deep waters of the Atlantic and Pacific
facts: It has changed so little over millions of years it is called a 'living fossil'.
It has about 300 needle-like, three-pronged teeth.
Its pregnancy may last up to 3.5 years, possibly the longest of any vertebrate.
Its six pairs of frilly gill slits give it its name.

name: Goblin shark
facts: It can shoot its jaws forward out of its mouth to snatch prey.
Its long, flat snout is covered in electroreceptors to detect prey.
Its skin is pinkish because blood vessels show through.
It is rarely seen alive.

name: Greenland shark
habitat: Deep, cold waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic
facts: It is the longest-lived vertebrate known, with some estimated to be around 400 years old.
It swims very slowly, usually under 3 km/h.
Its flesh is toxic when fresh but is fermented in Iceland to make hákarl.
Many have parasitic copepods attached to their eyes.

name: Sarcastic fringehead
facts: It defends its home by opening a huge, brightly coloured mouth.
Rivals 'mouth-wrestle' by pressing their open mouths together.
It often lives in empty shells or even discarded bottles.
It is only about 30 cm long, but very aggressive.

name: Ocean sunfish
facts: It is one of the heaviest bony fish, weighing up to over 2,000 kg.
A female can produce up to 300 million eggs at once.
It basks at the surface, possibly to warm up after deep dives.
Its tail is replaced by a rudder-like flap called a clavus.

name: Humpback anglerfish
facts: It lures prey with a glowing 'fishing rod' growing from its head.
The glow comes from bioluminescent bacteria living in the lure.
Its stretchy stomach and jaws let it swallow prey longer than itself.
Males are tiny compared with females.

name: Hagfish
facts: It can release large amounts of slime to clog predators' gills.
It can tie itself in a knot to clean off slime.
Hagfish slime is reinforced with incredibly fine protein threads, which researchers have studied as a model for new fibres.
It can go months without eating.

name: Coelacanth
habitat: Deep waters off southeastern Africa and Comoros
facts: It was thought extinct for 66 million years until found alive in 1938.
Its fleshy, lobed fins move in a pattern similar to walking.
It gives birth to live young.
It can live around 100 years.

name: Red-lipped batfish
facts: Its bright red lips may help individuals recognize each other during spawning.
It is a poor swimmer and 'walks' along the sea floor on its stiff pectoral and pelvic fins.
It has a small lure on its head, like its anglerfish relatives, to attract prey.
It is found mainly around the Galápagos Islands.

name: Weedy seadragon
facts: It looks like drifting seaweed.
The male carries eggs on his tail.
It is the marine emblem of Victoria.
It has no teeth and sucks up tiny shrimp.

name: Pacific lamprey
habitat: Pacific coast of North America and Asia
facts: It has no jaws, just a round sucker mouth lined with rows of horny teeth.
It attaches to fish and whales to feed on their blood and body fluids.
Lampreys have changed remarkably little for over 300 million years.
Like salmon, it migrates from the ocean up rivers to spawn, and adults die after spawning.

name: Christmas tree worm
facts: Its two colourful spiral crowns of tentacles look like tiny Christmas trees.
The 'trees' are feathery tentacles used for feeding and breathing.
It retracts instantly into its tube when disturbed.
It can live for over 40 years.

name: Bobbit worm
facts: It hides in the sea floor and ambushes prey with scissor-like jaws.
It can grow up to about 3 metres long.
Its strike is so fast it can slice fish in half.
It was named after the Bobbitt case in the 1990s.

name: Sea angel
habitat: Cold waters of the Arctic and North Atlantic
facts: It is a shell-less swimming sea snail, with a see-through body only a few centimetres long.
It 'flies' through the water by flapping two wing-like lobes.
It feeds almost exclusively on shelled sea butterflies, grabbing them with tentacles called buccal cones.
It can survive for months without eating when prey is scarce.

name: Vampire squid
facts: Its name means 'vampire squid from hell'.
It eats marine snow, not blood.
When threatened, it pulls its webbed arms up over its body, a defensive pose called the 'pineapple posture'.
It glows with bioluminescent organs.

name: Comb jelly
facts: Comb jellies swim using eight rows of beating hair-like cilia, the largest animals known to move this way.
The beating cilia scatter light, producing shimmering rainbow colours that are not bioluminescence.
Despite looking like jellyfish, they are a separate group and have no stinging cells.
An invasive comb jelly, Mnemiopsis, devastated fisheries in the Black Sea in the 1980s.

name: Portuguese man o' war
facts: It is not a single animal but a colony of specialized organisms called zooids.
Its tentacles can be over 30 metres long.
Its sail helps it drift with the wind.
Its sting is very painful.

name: Peacock spider
facts: Males dance and display colourful abdomens.
It is only a few millimetres long.
Males risk being eaten if the female dislikes the dance.
It belongs to the jumping spider family.

name: Orchid mantis
facts: It looks like an orchid flower.
It lures pollinating insects.
Its legs look like petals.
Females are much bigger than males.

name: Giant weta
facts: Giant weta are among the heaviest insects in the world.
Weta are related to crickets and grasshoppers.
Some can weigh more than a sparrow.
It is threatened by introduced predators.

name: Atlas moth
facts: It is one of the largest moths in the world.
Adults have no mouths and live only about a week.
Wing tips look like snake heads.
Its cocoons are used as purses in Taiwan.

name: Purple frog
facts: It spends almost its entire life underground, surfacing only for a few weeks during the monsoon to breed.
Its closest relatives live in the Seychelles, a link dating back to when India and the Seychelles were joined.
It was only formally described by scientists in 2003.
It eats termites using a grooved tongue, and its pointed snout helps it burrow.

name: Hairy frog
facts: Breeding males grow hair-like strands of skin on their flanks and thighs that help them absorb oxygen.
When threatened, it can break its own toe bones to push sharp claws out through its skin.
It is sometimes called the 'horror frog' or 'Wolverine frog'.
It is eaten as a delicacy in parts of Cameroon.

name: Glass frog
habitat: Forests of Central and northern South America
facts: Its belly skin is transparent, so you can see its heart, liver and gut.
Males guard eggs laid on leaves overhanging streams.
When tadpoles hatch, they drop into the water below.
While it sleeps, it can hide nearly 90% of its red blood cells in its liver, making itself even more transparent.

name: Mexican burrowing toad
facts: It looks like a small inflated balloon with a tiny pointed head.
It spends most of its life underground, emerging after heavy rains to breed.
It catches termites and ants by flicking its tongue straight out of the front of its mouth, unlike most frogs.
It is the only living member of its family.

name: Lake Titicaca water frog
facts: Its loose, baggy skin folds increase surface area so it can absorb oxygen from cold, high-altitude water.
It lives almost entirely underwater and rarely surfaces to breathe.
It is sometimes nicknamed the 'scrotum frog'.
It is critically endangered due to pollution and over-harvesting.

name: Olm
habitat: Underground cave waters of the Dinaric Alps in Europe
facts: This blind, pale salamander lives its whole life in dark cave waters.
It can live over 100 years.
It can survive up to 10 years without food.
Locals once thought it was a baby dragon washed out of caves by floods.

name: Chinese giant salamander
facts: It is among the largest amphibians in the world, reaching up to about 1.8 metres long.
It breathes mainly through its wrinkly skin.
It can make sounds like a crying baby, earning it the Chinese name 'baby fish'.
It is critically endangered, mainly from overharvesting for food.

name: Hellbender
habitat: Streams of the eastern United States
facts: It is North America's largest salamander.
Its flattened, wrinkly body has lots of skin folds to absorb oxygen from water.
It needs clean, fast-flowing, oxygen-rich water, so it is a good indicator of stream health.
It goes by colourful nicknames like 'snot otter' and 'lasagna lizard'.

name: Caecilian
facts: These limbless amphibians look like large earthworms or snakes.
Some species' babies feed by peeling off and eating their mother's specially thickened skin.
Most live underground and have tiny eyes covered by skin or bone.
They have a pair of sensory tentacles between their eyes and nostrils.

name: Satanic leaf-tailed gecko
facts: Its flattened tail looks exactly like a dead, decaying leaf, complete with notches.
It has no eyelids and licks its eyes to keep them clean.
Despite its name, it is harmless.
It is active at night and hides in vegetation during the day.

name: Armadillo girdled lizard
facts: When threatened, it bites its own tail and curls into a spiky ball, like an armadillo.
It lives in social groups, unusual for lizards.
Females give birth to live young, usually one or two at a time.
It sometimes raids termite nests for food.

name: Shingleback skink
habitat: Dry regions of southern and western Australia
facts: Its short, stubby tail looks like its head, confusing predators.
Pairs often stay together for many years, sometimes over 20.
It gives birth to live young, which are large relative to the mother.
It sticks out its blue tongue to scare predators.

name: Pig-nosed turtle
habitat: Rivers of northern Australia and New Guinea
facts: It has a pig-like nose that works as a snorkel.
Its flippers are more like those of sea turtles than freshwater turtles.
Its eggs only hatch when flooded, triggered by low oxygen levels.
It is the only living member of its family.

name: Mary River turtle
facts: It can breathe through glands in its rear end, letting it stay underwater for up to 3 days.
Some individuals grow algae on their heads, giving them green 'punk' hairstyles.
It is found in just one river system in the world.
Its numbers fell because its eggs were once collected for the pet trade.

name: Alligator snapping turtle
habitat: Rivers of the southeastern United States
facts: It has a worm-like lure on its tongue to attract fish into its mouth.
It is one of the heaviest freshwater turtles in the world.
It can stay underwater for up to 50 minutes.
Its strong jaws can deliver a powerful bite.

name: Gila monster
habitat: Deserts of the southwestern US and northwestern Mexico
facts: It is one of the few venomous lizards.
It stores fat in its tail, letting it go months without eating.
A compound in its saliva led to a drug for type 2 diabetes.
It spends most of its life underground.

name: Rhinoceros iguana
facts: Males have bony, horn-like bumps on their snouts, which give the species its name.
It is found only on the island of Hispaniola and nearby islets.
Males also develop a fatty pad on top of the head and a large dewlap.
It is mostly herbivorous, eating leaves, flowers and fruit.

name: Panther chameleon
facts: Its colour varies by region, and males from different localities can be red, blue, green or orange.
Its eyes can move independently, letting it look in two directions at once.
Its tongue can shoot out more than its own body length to catch insects.
Colour changes are produced by adjusting tiny crystals in its skin cells that reflect light.

name: Brookesia micra
facts: It is one of the smallest reptiles in the world, under 3 cm long including its tail.
Juveniles can comfortably stand on the head of a match.
It was described as a new species in 2012.
Its tiny size is thought to be an example of 'island dwarfism' on its small islet.

name: Draco lizard
facts: It glides on wing-like flaps of skin stretched over extendable ribs.
It can glide up to 60 metres.
Males have a colourful throat flap used for display.
It lives mostly in trees.

name: Spiny bush viper
facts: Its strongly keeled, upturned scales make it look shaggy, almost like a dragon.
It lives mostly in trees and shrubs, gripping branches with a prehensile tail.
It hunts small mammals, frogs and lizards at night.
Males are much longer than females, unusual among snakes.

name: Spider-tailed horned viper
facts: The tip of its tail ends in a bulb fringed with long scales that looks remarkably like a spider.
It wiggles the fake spider to lure insect-eating birds within striking range.
It was formally described as a new species only in 2006.
Its rough, sandy colouring camouflages it perfectly against rocky hillsides.

name: Saola
habitat: Annamite Mountains of Vietnam and Laos
facts: It was discovered by science only in 1992, one of the most spectacular large-mammal finds of the 20th century.
It is so rarely seen that it is nicknamed the 'Asian unicorn'.
Scientists have never confirmed a sighting of one in the wild; it is known mainly from camera traps and a handful of captured animals.
Large scent glands on its face may be used to mark territory.

name: Red panda
habitat: Himalayan forests of Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar and China
facts: It was described as a 'panda' about 50 years before the giant panda.
It has a 'false thumb', an extended wrist bone, for gripping bamboo.
It spends most of its day sleeping in trees.
It is not closely related to the giant panda but is in its own family.

name: Mountain tapir
habitat: Andes mountains of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru
facts: It has thick woolly fur to cope with cold mountain climates.
Its short trunk is a fusion of its nose and upper lip.
It is one of the smallest tapir species and the only one that lives outside tropical lowland forest.
It is an important seed disperser in the Andes.

name: Malayan tapir
facts: Its black-and-white colouring breaks up its outline in moonlit forests.
Babies are born with stripes and spots like watermelons.
It uses its trunk to grab leaves and fruit.
It is the largest tapir species.

name: Hispaniolan hutia
facts: It is one of the few native land mammals left on Hispaniola.
It is a large rodent that climbs trees.
It is mostly active at night.
It is threatened by introduced predators.

name: Philippine tarsier
facts: Each of its eyes is about as big as its brain.
It cannot move its eyes, so it rotates its head nearly 180 degrees.
It communicates with ultrasonic calls humans can't hear.
It is one of the smallest primates.

name: Sunda slow loris
facts: It is one of the very few venomous primates.
It licks venom from glands on its arms, mixing it with saliva.
It moves slowly and silently through trees.
It can hold onto branches for hours with a strong grip.

name: Golden snub-nosed monkey
facts: Its nose is so flat it looks almost missing.
It lives at high altitudes and endures snowy winters.
Its thick golden fur keeps it warm.
Groups can number in the hundreds.

name: Bald uakari
facts: Its bright red face is a sign of good health.
It has a short tail, unusual for New World monkeys.
It eats seeds with strong teeth.
It lives in flooded forests during the wet season.

name: Mandrill
facts: It is the world's largest monkey.
Dominant males have the brightest red-and-blue faces and rumps.
Its colours become more vivid when it is excited.
It can gather in groups called hordes of hundreds of individuals.

name: Gelada
facts: It is the only primate that eats mainly grass.
It has a bright red chest patch, sometimes called the 'bleeding heart'.
Herds of geladas can number over a thousand.
It sleeps on cliff ledges at night.

name: Indri
facts: It is one of the largest living lemurs.
Its haunting songs can be heard up to 2 km away.
Its calls have a rhythm, a rare trait in mammals.
It is critically endangered.

name: Verreaux's sifaka
facts: It moves on the ground by hopping sideways on its hind legs.
It can leap up to 10 metres between trees.
Its name comes from its alarm call.
It sunbathes in the morning to warm up.

name: Red-shanked douc
habitat: Forests of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia
facts: It is nicknamed the 'costumed ape' for its colourful fur.
It has maroon 'shorts' on its legs.
It eats mostly leaves.
It is endangered due to hunting.

name: Patagonian mara
facts: It looks like a cross between a rabbit and a deer.
It is a large rodent related to guinea pigs.
Pairs mate for life.
It can run up to 45 km/h.

name: Pacarana
facts: It is a slow-moving rodent with spots like a paca.
Its name means 'false paca'.
It is the only living member of its family.
It is rarely seen in the wild.

name: Kirk's dik-dik
facts: It is one of the smallest antelopes.
It is named after its alarm call.
Its long snout helps keep it cool.
Pairs mark their territory with dung piles.

name: Bongo
facts: It has bright chestnut fur with white stripes.
Both males and females have spiral horns.
It is one of the largest forest antelopes.
It is shy and rarely seen.

name: Lesser mouse-deer
facts: It is one of the smallest hoofed mammals.
Males have fang-like teeth instead of antlers.
It looks like a cross between a mouse and a deer.
It is a symbol of cleverness in Malay folklore.

name: Takin
facts: It is related to sheep and goats.
It secretes an oily substance to protect against rain.
It is the national animal of Bhutan.
It may have inspired the myth of the Golden Fleece.

name: Southern pudú
facts: It is one of the smallest deer in the world.
It stands only about 35-45 cm tall.
It climbs fallen logs to reach leaves.
Newborns are reddish-brown with white spots that fade as they grow.

name: Dugong
facts: It is a sea cow related to manatees, and its closest living land relatives are elephants.
It feeds almost entirely on seagrass, leaving feeding trails across the sea floor.
Unlike a manatee's paddle tail, its tail is fluked like a whale's.
Sightings by sailors may have helped inspire legends of mermaids.

name: Vaquita
facts: It is the world's smallest porpoise.
It is the most endangered marine mammal.
Surveys in 2024 estimated that fewer than ten remain, mainly due to drowning in illegal gillnets.
It has dark rings around its eyes.

name: Lowland streaked tenrec
facts: It is the only mammal known to communicate by stridulation, rubbing special quills on its back together to make sound.
The sound is mostly too high-pitched for humans to hear and helps family groups keep in touch while foraging.
Its black-and-yellow striped spines can detach and lodge in a predator's nose or mouth.
Despite looking like a tiny hedgehog, it belongs to a group of mammals more closely related to elephants and aardvarks.

name: Atlantic horseshoe crab
habitat: Atlantic coast of North America and the Gulf of Mexico
facts: It is not a true crab; it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions.
Horseshoe crabs have existed for over 400 million years, long before the dinosaurs.
Its blue, copper-based blood is used to make a test (LAL) that checks medicines and vaccines for bacterial contamination.
It has ten eyes, including simple eyes on its tail-facing shell that sense light.
